name: Titanium dioxide sunscreen

lead: Titanium dioxide sunscreens use a mineral filter that gives good protection against UVB and part of UVA, used for slower photoaging and less sun damage. It is usually paired with zinc oxide for fuller coverage.

Fine particles on the skin absorb UV light and scatter some of it. With zinc oxide it is one of the two filters the FDA classed as generally recognized as safe and effective as of 2021. It does not fully cover the UVA range, and some products add iron oxide to block visible light.

paras: People use it in mineral sunscreens and tinted daily creams, often ultrafine versions combined with zinc oxide, applied to the face and body before sun exposure.
White cast is a common cosmetic complaint. Inhaled TiO2 dust is classified Group 2B by IARC, which is why sprays draw caution. A 1990s pilot study looked at absorption through human skin.

angle.text: Titanium dioxide sunscreens are used for mineral-based protection, strongest against UVB and partly UVA, and are often paired with zinc oxide for fuller coverage. Less UV damage slows photoaging and keeps tone even.

lead: Titanium dioxide sunscreen uses titanium dioxide (TiO2), an inorganic mineral, as an ultraviolet filter. With zinc oxide it is one of the two mineral filters in sunscreens, and the two were the only filters the US FDA classed as generally recognized as safe and effective as of 2021.[1]

Wikipedia says titanium dioxide offers good protection but does not fully cover the UVA range.[1] Sunscreens use ultrafine (nanoscale) forms, often combined with ultrafine zinc oxide, and some add iron oxide to block visible light.[2]
Published work on the ingredient includes a 1990s pilot study of absorption through human skin, a yeast-based photosafety model, and patents on mineral powder blends.[3][4][5]

paras: Wikipedia describes mineral filters as working mainly by absorbing UV, with some reflection and scattering.[1] In plastics and other materials the article attributes TiO2's UV protection to light scattering from its high refractive index.[2] Because mineral products can leave a white cast, formulators use ultrafine particles and blends of particle sizes.[1][2][6]

A 1996 pilot study in Australia had patients scheduled for skin surgery apply microfine titanium dioxide sunscreen daily for 2 to 6 weeks beforehand and then analysed skin samples to assess percutaneous absorption, because the authors saw little prior data while the products were being widely recommended.[3]

The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies inhaled titanium dioxide dust as Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic to humans; Wikipedia says this concerns inhaled dust rather than sunscreen use directly, and that IARC recommends against sprayable sunscreens because of inhalation risk.[2] Wikipedia also says it is not yet known how well healthy skin blocks absorption, or whether damaged skin or prolonged use raises exposure.[2]

Nanoscale anatase TiO2 can produce hydroxyl radicals under UV, a property used in self-cleaning surfaces; sunscreen particles are generally coated.[2] A 2019 study used Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains as a model to assess photoprotective and photomutagenic effects of a titanium dioxide sunscreen.[4]
Environmentally, Wikipedia says most nanoparticles from cosmetics enter wastewater and about 99 percent of them end up on land in sewage sludge rather than in water.[2]

A 1996 pilot study in patients having skin surgery examined absorption of microfine titanium dioxide from sunscreen applied daily for 2 to 6 weeks.[3] No trials of appearance outcomes specific to titanium dioxide sunscreen were found.

timeline.event: Australian pilot study on percutaneous absorption of microfine TiO2 sunscreen.[3]
FDA lists titanium dioxide and zinc oxide as the only GRASE sunscreen filters.[1]
